claim: Premotor circuits in the brainstem project to pools of orofacial motoneurons to execute essential motor action such as licking, chewing, breathing, and in rodent, whisking.
source: Premotor circuits in the brainstem project to pools of orofacial motoneurons to execute essential motor action such as licking, chewing, breathing, and in rodent, whisking.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about premotor circuits and their function.

claim: Previous transsynaptic tracing studies only mapped orofacial premotor circuits in neonatal mice.
source: Previous transsynaptic tracing studies only mapped orofacial premotor circuits in neonatal mice, but the adult circuits remain unknown as a consequence of technical difficulties.
evidence: This statement references prior work and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adult orofacial premotor circuits remain unknown as a consequence of technical difficulties.
source: Previous transsynaptic tracing studies only mapped orofacial premotor circuits in neonatal mice, but the adult circuits remain unknown as a consequence of technical difficulties.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivated the current study.

claim: A three-step monosynaptic transsynaptic tracing strategy was developed to identify premotor neurons controlling vibrissa, tongue protrusion, and jaw-closing muscles in the adult mouse.
source: Here, we developed a three-step monosynaptic transsynaptic tracing strategy to identify premotor neurons controlling vibrissa, tongue protrusion, and jaw-closing muscles in the adult mouse.
evidence: This is a primary methodological claim supported by the detailed methods and results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different groups of premotor neurons were registered onto the Allen mouse brain common coordinate framework (CCF).
source: We registered these different groups of premotor neurons onto the Allen mouse brain common coordinate framework (CCF) and consequently generated a combined 3D orofacial premotor atlas, revealing unique spatial organizations of distinct premotor circuits.
evidence: This is supported by the methods and results showing registration procedures and visualizations in CCF.

claim: A combined 3D orofacial premotor atlas was generated revealing unique spatial organizations of distinct premotor circuits.
source: We registered these different groups of premotor neurons onto the Allen mouse brain common coordinate framework (CCF) and consequently generated a combined 3D orofacial premotor atlas, revealing unique spatial organizations of distinct premotor circuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the 3D reconstructions and spatial analyses presented in the results.

claim: Premotor neurons that simultaneously innervate multiple motor nuclei were uncovered.
source: We further uncovered premotor neurons that simultaneously innervate multiple motor nuclei and, consequently, are likely to coordinate different muscles involved in the same orofacial motor actions.
evidence: This is supported by axon collateral tracing and split-Cre experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Premotor neurons that simultaneously innervate multiple motor nuclei are likely to coordinate different muscles involved in the same orofacial motor actions.
source: We further uncovered premotor neurons that simultaneously innervate multiple motor nuclei and, consequently, are likely to coordinate different muscles involved in the same orofacial motor actions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical connectivity data presented.

claim: The method for tracing adult premotor circuits and registering to Allen CCF is generally applicable.
source: Our method for tracing adult premotor circuits and registering to Allen CCF is generally applicable and should facilitate the investigations of motor controls of diverse behaviors.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the method based on its successful application.

claim: Orofacial motor actions underlie breathing, drinking, and eating, which are essential for animals to access vital sustenance.
source: Orofacial motor actions, which underlie breathing, drinking, and eating, are essential for animals to access vital sustenance, that is, oxygen, water, and food (Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mice use coordinated whisking and sniffing, often in coordination with breathing, to explore their physical environment.
source: Mice, as nocturnal animals, use coordinated whisking and sniffing, often in coordination with breathing, to explore their physical environment (Deschênes et al., 2012; Kleinfeld and Deschenes, 2011; Moore et al., 2014; Welker, 1964).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many orofacial behaviors utilize multiple muscles through coordinated activity of their associated motoneurons.
source: Thus, many of the orofacial behaviors utilize multiple muscles through coordinated activity of their associated motoneurons in a seamless manner (Kurnikova et al., 2017; McElvain et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Each orofacial motoneuron pool only projects to its corresponding muscle and lacks collaterals to innervate other central neurons.
source: Given that each orofacial motoneuron pool only projects to its corresponding muscle and lacks collaterals to innervate other central neurons, and that individual motor actions may involve multiple muscles, coordinated orofacial behaviors are thought to be achieved by orofacial premotor circuits in the brainstem (Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Coordinated orofacial behaviors are thought to be achieved by orofacial premotor circuits in the brainstem.
source: Given that each orofacial motoneuron pool only projects to its corresponding muscle and lacks collaterals to innervate other central neurons, and that individual motor actions may involve multiple muscles, coordinated orofacial behaviors are thought to be achieved by orofacial premotor circuits in the brainstem (Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical constraints and is supported by a citation.

claim: Putative premotor neurons that project to different craniofacial motor nuclei had been previously mapped using conventional retrograde tracers.
source: Putative premotor neurons that project to different craniofacial motor nuclei had been previously mapped using conventional retrograde tracers injected into different motor nuclei in the brainstem (Borke et al., 1983; Hattox et al., 2002; Isokawa-Akesson and Komisaruk, 1987; Travers and Norgren, 1983; Vornov and Sutin, 1983).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each orofacial motor nucleus contains functionally different and also antagonistic motor neurons.
source: However, each orofacial motor nucleus contains functionally different and also antagonistic motor neurons (Aldes, 1995; Ashwell, 1982; Klein and Rhoades, 1985; Krammer et al., 1979; Mizuno et al., 1975).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The hypoglossal nucleus contains motoneurons for tongue protrusion, retrusion, and shaping.
source: For instance, the hypoglossal nucleus contains motoneurons for tongue protrusion, retrusion, and shaping.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Conventional retrograde tracers lack muscle/motoneuron specificity.
source: Thus, a major limitation of conventional tracers is the lack of muscle/motoneuron specificity.
evidence: This is a critique of conventional methods based on their technical limitations.

claim: Transsynaptic viral tracers injected into specific muscle groups identify presynaptic nuclei but suffer from the uncertainty of labeling higher order in addition to presynaptic nuclei.
source: An improvement is the injection of transsynaptic viral tracers into specific muscle groups, such as replication-competent rabies (Kurnikova et al., 2019) and pseudorabies (Mercer Lindsay et al., 2019). This approach identifies presynaptic nuclei but suffers from the uncertainty of labeling higher order in addition to presynaptic nuclei.
evidence: This is a critique of an alternative method supported by citations.

claim: Monosynaptic retrograde rabies virus transsynaptic tracing strategy was used to examine premotor circuits for various craniofacial and somatic motoneurons in neonatal mice.
source: To overcome such limitations, we and others used a monosynaptic retrograde rabies virus transsynaptic tracing strategy and examined the premotor circuits for various craniofacial and somatic motoneurons in neonatal mice (Sreenivasan et al., 2015; Stanek et al., 2014; Stepien et al., 2010; Takatoh et al., 2013; Tripodi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work by the authors and others, supported by citations.

claim: ΔG-RV does not infect from peripheral muscles efficiently in animals older than P8.
source: However, ∆G-RV does not infect from peripheral muscles efficiently in animals older than P8, thus precluding the use of this strategy to trace premotor circuits beyond approximately P15 (Takatoh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a technical limitation observed in prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Many orofacial behaviors do not fully develop until after weaning.
source: Since many orofacial behaviors do not fully develop until after weaning (Westneat and Hall, 1992), it is uncertain whether the orofacial premotor circuits revealed for neonatal mice are the same in adult animals, at age at which most of the behavior and electrophysiology experiments are conducted.
evidence: This is established developmental knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It is uncertain whether the orofacial premotor circuits revealed for neonatal mice are the same in adult animals.
source: Since many orofacial behaviors do not fully develop until after weaning (Westneat and Hall, 1992), it is uncertain whether the orofacial premotor circuits revealed for neonatal mice are the same in adult animals, at age at which most of the behavior and electrophysiology experiments are conducted.
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental considerations and technical limitations.

claim: AAV2-retro-Cre is injected into motoneurons innervating specific muscles through intramuscular injection in juvenile mice as the first step of the three-step strategy.
source: First, we introduce Cre recombinase into motoneurons innervating specific muscles through the intramuscular injection of the highly efficient retrograde viral vector AAV2-retro-Cre (Tervo et al., 2016) in juvenile mice.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the first step of the tracing strategy.

claim: Cre-dependent AAV expressing TVA receptor and optimized rabies glycoprotein oG is injected into corresponding brainstem motor nuclei in adult mice as the second step.
source: Second, in adult mice, we inject Cre-dependent AAV that expresses the TVA receptor and the optimized rabies glycoprotein oG (AAV-Flex-TVA-mCherry [Miyamichi et al., 2013] and AAV-Flex-oG [Kim et al., 2016]) into the corresponding brainstem motor nuclei in adult mice.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the second step of the tracing strategy.

claim: EnvA(M21)-RV-ΔG-GFP only infects TVA-expressing motoneurons.
source: Finally, we inject the pseudotyped EnvA-∆G-RV-GFP, which only infect TVA-expressing motoneurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the specificity of the viral vector used.

claim: EnvA(M21)-RV-ΔG-GFP spreads into corresponding premotor neurons through the complementation of oG five days after injection.
source: Five days later, through the complementation of oG, the virus will spread into the corresponding premotor neurons (Wickersham et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of transsynaptic spread, supported by a citation.

claim: AAV2-retro-Cre injected early in postnatal days (~P10) into the mystacial pad resulted in widespread labeling including neurons in medial and middle parts of FN.
source: When we injected AAV2-retro-Cre early in postnatal days (~P10) into the mystacial pad, we observed widespread labeling. In addition to motoneurons located in the lateral part of FN that innervates the mystacial pad, neurons in the medial and middle parts of FN were also labeled, likely through entering the fluid of the peri-nerve space after injection and subsequently infecting other motor axons in the same nerve.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the age of the mouse advanced, retrogradely labeled neurons became progressively restricted to the lateral part of FN and the number of labeled neurons drastically decreased.
source: As the age of the mouse advanced, the retrogradely labeled neurons became progressively restricted to the lateral part of FN and the number of labeled neurons also drastically decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AAV2-retro-Cre was injected in desired craniofacial muscles at P17 to achieve specificity and good efficiency of infection.
source: We, therefore, decided to inject AAV2-retro-Cre in the desired craniofacial muscles at P17 as step 1, which gave us specificity and good efficiency of infection.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on optimization experiments.

claim: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the Bötzinger complex (BötC)/retrofacial region.
source: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the Bötzinger complex (BötC)/retrofacial region (Figure 2A), the vibrissa zone of the IRt (vIRt) (Figure 2B), and the dorsal medullary reticular nucleus (MdD) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the vibrissa premotor tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the vibrissa zone of the IRt (vIRt).
source: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the Bötzinger complex (BötC)/retrofacial region (Figure 2A), the vibrissa zone of the IRt (vIRt) (Figure 2B), and the dorsal medullary reticular nucleus (MdD) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the vibrissa premotor tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the dorsal medullary reticular nucleus (MdD).
source: The densest labeling of vibrissa premotor neurons was found in the Bötzinger complex (BötC)/retrofacial region (Figure 2A), the vibrissa zone of the IRt (vIRt) (Figure 2B), and the dorsal medullary reticular nucleus (MdD) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the vibrissa premotor tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The BötC/retrofacial region is known to contain expiration-rhythmic cells.
source: The BötC/retrofacial that region resides immediately posterior to FN is known to contain expiration-rhythmic cells (Deschênes et al., 2016a) and is implicated in the control of sniffing behavior that is often coupled with whisking during exploration (Deschênes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The BötC/retrofacial region is implicated in the control of sniffing behavior that is often coupled with whisking during exploration.
source: The BötC/retrofacial that region resides immediately posterior to FN is known to contain expiration-rhythmic cells (Deschênes et al., 2016a) and is implicated in the control of sniffing behavior that is often coupled with whisking during exploration (Deschênes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The vIRt is known to contain whisking oscillator cells.
source: The vIRt, located medial to the compact part of the nucleus ambiguus (cNA), is known to contain whisking oscillator cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of vIRt.

claim: A few premotor neurons were consistently observed in the preBötzinger complex (preBötC).
source: A few premotor neurons were also consistently observed in the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) (Figure 2B), which is reported to entrain whisking and sniffing (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the vibrissa premotor tracing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The preBötC is reported to entrain whisking and sniffing.
source: A few premotor neurons were also consistently observed in the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) (Figure 2B), which is reported to entrain whisking and sniffing (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Vibrissa premotor neurons were labeled in the ipsilateral deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN) interpositus in adult mice.
source: First, vibrissa premotor neurons were labeled in the ipsilateral deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN) interpositus (Figure 2I) in the adult mouse, which were not present in juvenile animals.
evidence: This is a finding from adult tracing shown in Figure 2I, compared to neonatal results.

claim: Vibrissa premotor neurons in the ipsilateral DCN interpositus were not present in juvenile animals.
source: First, vibrissa premotor neurons were labeled in the ipsilateral deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN) interpositus (Figure 2I) in the adult mouse, which were not present in juvenile animals.
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and neonatal tracing results.

claim: Premotor neurons were not found in the spinal vestibular nucleus in adult mice, although this was observed in perinatal tracing.
source: Second, we did not find premotor neurons in the spinal vestibular nucleus in adult mice, although this was observed in perinatal tracing.
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and neonatal tracing results.

claim: Labeled neurons were observed in the zona incerta (ZI) and in extended amygdala in adult that were not labeled in the neonatal transsynaptic tracing studies.
source: Finally, we observed labeled neurons in the zona incerta (ZI) and in extended amygdala in adult that were not labeled in the neonatal transsynaptic tracing studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,C'; Takatoh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and neonatal tracing results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greatest number of labeled tongue-protruding premotor neurons was found bilaterally in the dorsal IRt.
source: Qualitatively, the greatest number of labeled tongue-protruding premotor neurons was found bilaterally in the dorsal IRt (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genioglossus premotor tracing shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tongue-protruding premotor neurons in dorsal IRt spread along the anterior-posterior axis with the highest density in the area anterior to the rostral edge of the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: These neurons spread along the anterior-posterior axis of the dorsal IRt with the highest density in the area anterior to the rostral edge of the hypoglossal nucleus (see the details of IRt organization in the section below).
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of labeled neurons.

claim: Many labeled cells with very large soma size were found in Gi/LPGi/LRt areas, spanning along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Many labeled cells with very large soma size were found in Gi/LPGi/LRt areas, spanning along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the genioglossus premotor tracing shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Labeled tongue premotor neurons were observed in the dorsal part of the principal trigeminal nucleus (PrV).
source: In the sensory-related areas, labeled tongue premotor neurons were observed in the dorsal part of the principal trigeminal nucleus (PrV) (Figure 3C), nucleus of solitary tract (NST), and dorsomedial SpV (DMSpV) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the genioglossus premotor tracing shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Labeled neurons resided in the medial subnucleus of DCN in the tongue premotor circuit.
source: In the cerebellum, labeled neurons resided in the medial subnucleus of DCN (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a finding from the genioglossus premotor tracing shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The large cluster of premotor neurons in the dorsal midbrain reticular formation (dMRf) previously found in juvenile animals was absent in adult mice.
source: However, in adult mice, the large cluster of premotor neurons in the dorsal midbrain reticular formation (dMRf) previously found in juvenile animals (Stanek et al., 2014) was absent in adult mice.
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and juvenile tracing results.

claim: In the masseter premotor circuit, extensive labeling was found bilaterally along the anterior-posterior axis of the dorsal IRt.
source: Qualitatively, in the masseter premotor circuit, extensive labeling was also found bilaterally along the anterior-posterior axis of the dorsal IRt (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the masseter premotor tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: The majority of labeled dorsal IRt neurons in the masseter premotor circuit were observed contralaterally in the caudal part of IRt.
source: Interestingly, the majority of labeled dorsal IRt neurons were observed contralaterally in the caudal part of IRt (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the masseter premotor tracing shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A distinct bilateral cluster of large-size neurons with medially directed dendrites was found around the PCRt/PrV area immediately caudal to the trigeminal motor nucleus in the masseter premotor circuit.
source: Rostrally, we found a distinct bilateral cluster of large-size neurons with medially directed dendrites situated around the PCRt/PrV area immediately caudal to the trigeminal motor nucleus (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the masseter premotor tracing shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Labeled cells resided bilaterally in the dorsal PrV in the masseter premotor circuit.
source: In the sensory-related areas, labeled cells resided bilaterally in the dorsal PrV (Figure 4E), ipsilaterally in the dorsomedial SpV (Figure 4A), and ipsilaterally in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the masseter premotor tracing shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Labeled neurons were identified in the contralateral medial subnucleus of DCN in the masseter premotor circuit.
source: Lastly, within the cerebellum, we identified labeled neurons in the contralateral medial subnucleus of DCN (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the masseter premotor tracing shown in Figure 4G.

claim: RV-traced GFP-positive premotor neurons were mapped onto the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv3).
source: To generate a standardized orofacial premotor atlas that enables cross-comparison of different premotor circuits, RV-traced GFP-positive premotor neurons were mapped onto the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv3) (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by the registration procedures described.

claim: The CCF is a widely used open-access three-dimensional standardized brain atlas generated from the average of 1675 adult C57BL/6J mice.
source: The CCF is a widely used open-access three-dimensional standardized brain atlas generated from the average of 1675 adult C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: This is a description of the CCF atlas supported by a citation.

claim: All traced orofacial motor neurons for vibrissa (four mice), genioglossus (four mice), and masseter (four mice) were registered to the CCF.
source: All traced orofacial motor neurons for vibrissa (four mice), genioglossus (four mice), and masseter (four mice) were registered to the CCF, and their coordinates are accessible from the source file.
evidence: This is a statement about the data processing and availability.

claim: Individual premotor tracing results from the same muscle/motor unit were highly correlated.
source: Individual premotor tracing results from the same muscle/motor unit were highly correlated, whereas results obtained from different muscles/motor units showed low correlations in spatial patterns (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Results obtained from different muscles/motor units showed low correlations in spatial patterns.
source: Individual premotor tracing results from the same muscle/motor unit were highly correlated, whereas results obtained from different muscles/motor units showed low correlations in spatial patterns (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All three premotor circuits showed the highest density of labeling in the intermediate and parvicellular reticular formations (IRt and PCRt).
source: All three premotor circuits showed the highest density of labeling in the intermediate and parvicellular reticular formations (IRt and PCRt); however, the exact peak density positions were in the different locations of IRt/PCRt for different circuits.
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis of the three premotor circuits.

claim: The exact peak density positions were in different locations of IRt/PCRt for different circuits.
source: All three premotor circuits showed the highest density of labeling in the intermediate and parvicellular reticular formations (IRt and PCRt); however, the exact peak density positions were in the different locations of IRt/PCRt for different circuits.
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis showing differential spatial organization.

claim: The vibrissa premotor circuit showed highest labeling density in the caudoventral areas of IRt.
source: The vibrissa premotor circuit showed highest labeling density in the caudoventral areas of IRt (Figure 5D, red).
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The masseter premotor circuit had densest labeling in the anterodorsal area of IRt.
source: The masseter premotor circuit had densest labeling in the anterodorsal area of IRt (Figure 5D, yellow).
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The highest density area of the genioglossus premotor neurons is located in IRt between the peaks for the vibrissa and masseter premotor cells (along the A–P axis).
source: The highest density area of the genioglossus premotor neurons is located in IRt between the peaks for the vibrissa and masseter premotor cells (along the A–P axis), although there were shared regions between genioglossus and masseter premotor distributions (Figure 5D, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There were shared regions between genioglossus and masseter premotor distributions.
source: The highest density area of the genioglossus premotor neurons is located in IRt between the peaks for the vibrissa and masseter premotor cells (along the A–P axis), although there were shared regions between genioglossus and masseter premotor distributions (Figure 5D, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the density analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Adult tracing results indicate IRt as the common area of premotor neurons for all three circuits.
source: Our adult tracing results indicate IRt as the common area of premotor neurons for all three circuits.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the spatial analysis of all three circuits.

claim: Earlier studies have either localized or implicated IRt as the region containing oscillator neurons for several orofacial actions, that is, whisking, licking, and chewing rhythm.
source: Earlier studies have either localized or implicated IRt as the region containing oscillator neurons for several orofacial actions, that is, whisking, licking, and chewing rhythm.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field.

claim: Three-dimensional reconstructions revealed partial overlapping and partial segregation of the three premotor circuits within IRt.
source: These three-dimensional reconstructions revealed partial overlapping and partial segregation of the three premotor circuits (Figure 6A-C).
evidence: This is a finding from the 3D reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The highest density regions of ipsilateral jaw-closing and tongue-protruding premotor neurons in IRt were close to each other, but with the peak of jaw premotor neurons shifted rostrally and ventrally.
source: Along the A–P axis, the highest density regions of ipsilateral jaw-closing and tongue-protruding premotor neurons in IRt were close to each other, but with the peak of jaw premotor neurons shifted rostrally and ventrally (Figure 6G-O , jaw peak: AP –6.02 ± 0.18 mm, DV –6.45 ± 0.04 mm; four mice, tongue peak: AP –6.20 ± 0.23 mm, DV –5.74 ± 0.29; four mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The contralateral jaw IRt premotor neurons formed a discernible cluster caudal to the densest area of tongue IRt premotor neurons, displaying a bilaterally asymmetric distribution.
source: Notably, the contralateral jaw IRt premotor neurons formed a discernible cluster caudal to the densest area of tongue IRt premotor neurons, displaying a bilaterally asymmetric distribution (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Vibrissa premotor neurons were more spatially separated from tongue and jaw premotor neurons in IRt, at more caudal and ventral locations.
source: Vibrissa premotor neurons were more spatially separated from tongue and jaw premotor neurons in IRt, that is, at more caudal and ventral (AP –6.45 ± 0.19 mm, DV –6.45 ± 0.04 mm; four mice) locations in IRt (Figure 6D-F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The tongue and jaw IRt premotor neurons showed similar densities between the ipsilateral and contralateral side.
source: Furthermore, the tongue and jaw IRt premotor neurons showed similar densities between the ipsilateral and contralateral side, which might be expected as licking and chewing generally involve muscles of both sides.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis with an interpretation.

claim: The vibrissa IRt premotor neurons showed biased distribution to the ipsilateral side.
source: In contrast, the vibrissa IRt premotor neurons showed biased distribution to the ipsilateral side (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Functionally distinct groups of orofacial premotor neurons occupy overlapping yet distinct spatial positions within IRt.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that functionally distinct groups of orofacial premotor neurons occupy the overlapping yet distinct spatial positions within IRt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of the three circuits.

claim: There is roughly a ventral-to-dorsal and caudal-to-rostral gradient of vibrissa-tongue-jaw premotor neurons.
source: Further, there is roughly a ventral-to-dorsal and caudal-to-rostral gradient of vibrissa-tongue-jaw premotor neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial organization pattern observed.

claim: Axonal collaterals from a fraction of labeled premotor neurons in genioglossus premotor tracing studies were found in the middle part of the FN, VIImiddle.
source: Interestingly, in genioglossus premotor tracing studies, axonal collaterals from a fraction of labeled premotor neurons were found in the middle part of the FN, VIImiddle (Figure 7B), where motor neurons controlling lip and jaw (platysma) movements reside.
evidence: This is a finding from axon collateral visualization shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Axon collaterals from genioglossus premotor neurons were found densely innervating the small subnucleus of the trigeminal motor nucleus, VAD, which controls the jaw-opening anterior digastric muscles.
source: Axon collaterals were also found densely innervating the small subnucleus of the trigeminal motor nucleus, VAD (Figure 7C and C'), which controls the jaw-opening anterior digastric muscles, as well as were observed in the accessory FN (data not shown), which innervates the posterior digastric jaw-opening muscle.
evidence: This is a finding from axon collateral visualization shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Certain premotor neurons that control tongue protrusion also simultaneously control mouth- and jaw opening through their axon collaterals.
source: These results suggest that certain premotor neurons that control tongue protrusion also simultaneously control mouth- and jaw opening through their axon collaterals, providing a neuronal substrate for coordinating multiple motor groups needed for proper execution of behaviors such as licking and feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the axon collateral data.

claim: Axonal collaterals from a fraction of labeled jaw-closing premotor neurons were observed in VIImiddle.
source: Similar to the above case for tongue-tracing studies, in masseter premotor tracing studies, the axonal collaterals from a fraction of labeled jaw-closing premotor neurons were observed in VIImiddle (Figure 7D) (same region receiving innervations from the tongue premotor neurons), in the contralateral trigeminal motor nucleus (Figure 7E), and densely in the dorsal part of the hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 7F), where motor neurons for tongue retrusion reside.
evidence: This is a finding from axon collateral visualization shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Premotor neurons controlling jaw-closing muscle also simultaneously modulate the tongue retrusion and likely mouth closing muscles through their axon collaterals.
source: These data provide additional evidence that premotor neurons controlling jaw-closing muscle also simultaneously modulate the tongue retrusion and likely mouth closing muscles through their axon collaterals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the axon collateral data.

claim: Collaterals from vibrissa premotor neurons project to the contralateral later FN where vibrissa motoneurons reside.
source: Finally, we also observed that collaterals from vibrissa premotor neurons project to the contralateral later FN where vibrissa motoneurons reside (Figure 7A), but not to hypoglossal and trigeminal motor nuclei.
evidence: This is a finding from axon collateral visualization shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Collaterals from vibrissa premotor neurons likely coordinate bilateral control of vibrissa set-point.
source: The former projections likely coordinate bilateral control of vibrissa set-point (Kleinfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the axon collateral data supported by a citation.

claim: Retrograde split-Cre tracing revealed tdTomato-positive cells in SupV and the dorsal IRt areas.
source: Retrograde split-Cre tracing revealed tdTomato-positive cells in SupV and the dorsal IRt areas (four mice, Figure 7K and L), where genioglossus premotor neurons were found (Figure 3A, B and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the split-Cre tracing experiments shown in Figure 7K and L.

claim: VIImiddle-XII common premotor neurons located in SupV and dorsal IRt simultaneously innervate motoneurons controlling tongue protrusion, lower lip, jaw opening, and throat.
source: Thus, VIImiddle-XII common premotor neurons located in SupV and dorsal IRt simultaneously innervate motoneurons controlling tongue protrusion, lower lip, jaw opening, and throat (through the nucleus ambiguus) (Figure 7O and P), suggesting that those common premotor neurons likely represent a fundamental neural substrate for coactivating these muscles.
evidence: This is a finding from the split-Cre tracing with an interpretation shown in Figure 7.

claim: SupV and dorsal IRt regions may be critical brainstem hubs that contain common premotor neurons that coordinate multiple groups of motoneurons for orofacial feeding behaviors.
source: These results indicate that SupV and dorsal IRt regions may be critical brainstem hubs that contain common premotor neurons that coordinate multiple groups of motoneurons for orofacial feeding behaviors (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the split-Cre tracing results shown in Figure 7P.

claim: A three-step monosynaptic RV tracing was developed to trace the premotor circuits for three different orofacial muscles in adult mice.
source: We developed a three-step monosynaptic RV tracing to trace the premotor circuits for three different orofacial muscles in adult mice (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution shown in Figure 8.

claim: The common atlas uncovers the overlapping yet distinct spatial organizations of premotor neurons involved in controlling movements of vibrissae, the tongue, and the jaw.
source: This common atlas uncovers the overlapping yet distinct spatial organizations of premotor neurons involved in controlling movements of vibrissae, the tongue, and the jaw.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the atlas.

claim: Visualization of premotor neurons' axon collaterals and retrograde split-Cre tracing studies highlighted premotor neurons in SupV and dorsal IRt as potential substrates for coordinating multiple distinct orofacial muscles involved in feeding-related behaviors.
source: Visualization of premotor neurons' axon collaterals and retrograde split-Cre tracing studies further highlighted premotor neurons in SupV and dorsal IRt as potential substrates for coordinating multiple distinct orofacial muscles involved in feeding-related behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the axon collateral and split-Cre experiments.

claim: The vibrissa premotor atlas consists of the most numerous brain structures among the three orofacial premotor circuits in adult mice.
source: Among the three orofacial premotor circuits in adult mice that we have mapped, the vibrissa premotor atlas consists of the most numerous brain structures (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the atlas shown in Figure 8.

claim: Vibrissa movements are needed for tactile exploration of complex physical environments.
source: This is not surprising since vibrissa movements, as opposed to more stereotyped licking and chewing, are needed for tactile exploration of complex physical environments (Mehta and Kleinfeld, 2004; Prescott et al., 2011; Sofroniew and Svoboda, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Two previous studies uncovered vIRt as the region containing vibrissa oscillator neurons.
source: Two previous studies uncovered vIRt as the region containing vibrissa oscillator neurons (Deschênes et al., 2016b; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies revealed the coupling between breathing/sniffing and whisking.
source: Previous studies also revealed the coupling between breathing/sniffing and whisking (Moore et al., 2013; Welker, 1964).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Premotor cells were traced in two brainstem areas known to control the respiratory rhythm, the retrofacial/BötC and preBötC.
source: Along this line, we traced premotor cells in two brainstem areas known to control the respiratory rhythm, that is, the retrofacial/BötC and preBötC (in both juvenile and adult mice), suggesting their roles in coordinating breathing and whisking, and potentially resetting the whisking rhythm (Kleinfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the tracing experiments with an interpretation.

claim: PreBötC innervates vIRt and is likely pre-premotor for vibrissa motoneurons.
source: PreBötC innervates vIRt; therefore, preBötC is likely pre-premotor for vibrissa motoneurons (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on connectivity data supported by a citation.

claim: Dorsal IRt near the rostral end of the hypoglossal nucleus contains the highest density of tongue-protruding premotor neurons.
source: In the tongue-protruding premotor circuit, dorsal IRt near the rostral end of the hypoglossal nucleus contains the highest density of premotor neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the genioglossus premotor tracing.

claim: Dorsal IRt has previously been implicated as the rhythm generator for licking.
source: This area has previously been implicated as the rhythm generator for licking.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field.

claim: Neurons in dorsal IRt show rhythmic activity that is phase-locked to licking in awake rats.
source: Using extracellular recording in awake rats, Travers et al. demonstrated that neurons in this area show rhythmic activity that is phase-locked to licking (Travers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Bilateral infusion of muscimol in dorsal IRt reduces licking electromyogram amplitude with minimal effect on the licking frequency.
source: However, bilateral infusion of muscimol in this area reduces licking electromyogram amplitude with minimal effect on the licking frequency (Chen et al., 2001; Travers et al., 2010), raising the possibility that dorsal IRt cells are the output of the actual licking oscillator.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Bilateral infusion of muscimol in the same IRt area also suppresses chewing/mastication.
source: Importantly, bilateral infusion of muscimol in the same IRt area also suppresses chewing/mastication, indicating the function of the dorsal IRt for coordination of tongue and jaw during ingestion behaviors.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work with an interpretation.

claim: Bilateral infusion of µ-opioid receptor agonist, DAMGO, in the dorsolateral IRt/rostral NST reduces licking frequency with increased amplitude.
source: Interestingly, bilateral infusion of µ-opioid receptor agonist, DAMGO, in the dorsolateral IRt/rostral NST reduces licking frequency with increased amplitude (Kinzeler and Travers, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Two regions, the dorsal IRt and PCRt between the rostral extent of the FN and the rostral extent of the hypoglossal nucleus, contain the highest numbers of jaw-closing premotor cells.
source: In the jaw-closing premotor circuit, two regions, the dorsal IRt and PCRt between the rostral extent of the FN and the rostral extent of the hypoglossal nucleus, contain the highest numbers of premotor cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the masseter premotor tracing.

claim: The IRt/PCRt area has been implicated as a critical node for generating chewing rhythm.
source: This IRt/PCRt area has been implicated as a critical node for generating chewing rhythm (Chandler et al., 1990; Nakamura et al., 2017; Nozaki et al., 1986b; Nozaki et al., 1986a; Travers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Stimulation of the cortical masticatory area induces rhythmic activity in the oral part of the gigantocellular (Gi) reticular nucleus (Go) in guinea pigs.
source: Nozaki et al. used a fictive rhythmic chewing preparation in guinea pigs to show that stimulation of the cortical masticatory area induces rhythmic activity in what was at the time called the oral part of the gigantocellular (Gi) reticular nucleus (Go).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Muscimol infusion in rostral IRt/PCRt but not Go suppresses neuropeptide Y-induced chewing behavior in awake rats.
source: More recently, Travers et al. demonstrated in awake rats that muscimol infusion in rostral IRt/PCRt but not Go suppresses neuropeptide Y-induced chewing behavior (Travers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Infusion of bicuculline in the IRt/PCRt area evokes chewing in awake mice.
source: Nakamura et al. used awake mice to show that infusion of bicuculline in the same IRt/PCRt area evokes chewing (Nakamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons in the dorsal PrV generate rhythmic bursting in brainstem slices spontaneously and upon electrical stimulation of the trigeminal tract.
source: Other studies showed that neurons in the dorsal PrV generate rhythmic bursting in brainstem slices spontaneously and upon electrical stimulation of the trigeminal tract (Morquette et al., 2015; Sandler et al., 1998), and during fictive chewing in anaesthetized and paralyzed rabbits (Tsuboi et al., 2003), suggesting the role of this area for chewing rhythm generation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in the lateral edge of PCRt respond to either noxious stimulation of the tongue or to light mechanical stimulation of intra- or perioral structures in cats.
source: Neurons in this area in cats respond to either noxious stimulation of the tongue or to light mechanical stimulation of intra- or perioral structures, including the teeth, gingiva, and lip.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Premotor neurons in SpVO and the supratrigeminal nucleus share the same masticatory rhythm during cortically induced fictive mastication in rats.
source: Inoue et al. demonstrated in rats that premotor neurons in SpVO and the supratrigeminal nucleus share the same masticatory rhythm during cortically induced fictive mastication (Inoue et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Premotor neurons in SpVO integrate sensory information from the oral area and rhythmic activity generated by a central rhythm generator to produce appropriate activity patterns during mastication.
source: Based on these properties, it is suggested that premotor neurons in SpVO integrate sensory information from the oral area and rhythmic activity generated by a central rhythm generator to produce appropriate activity patterns during mastication.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on prior work.

claim: Common premotor neurons in SupV and dorsal IRt may serve the simplest form of neuronal substrate for coordinating feeding-related orofacial behaviors by broadcasting rhythmic information of licking and chewing to synergistic muscles.
source: Common premotor neurons in SupV and dorsal IRt, therefore, may serve the simplest form of neuronal substrate for coordinating feeding-related orofacial behaviors by means of broadcasting rhythmic information of licking and chewing to synergistic muscles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the common premotor neuron findings.

claim: New additions of presynaptic inputs to control vibrissa motoneurons from ZI, DCN, and extended amygdala were observed in adult compared to neonatal circuits.
source: Comparing to neonatal circuits, we observed new additions of presynaptic inputs to control vibrissa motoneurons from ZI, DCN, and extended amygdala, and loss of presynaptic inputs from dMRf to tongue and jaw motoneurons in the adult premotor circuits (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and neonatal tracing results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Loss of presynaptic inputs from dMRf to tongue and jaw motoneurons was observed in adult compared to neonatal circuits.
source: Comparing to neonatal circuits, we observed new additions of presynaptic inputs to control vibrissa motoneurons from ZI, DCN, and extended amygdala, and loss of presynaptic inputs from dMRf to tongue and jaw motoneurons in the adult premotor circuits (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a comparison between adult and neonatal tracing results shown in Figure 8.

claim: These changes may reflect more fine-tuned control of tactile sensation by the vibrissae, and changes in feeding behaviors from neonatal suckling to adult licking and chewing.
source: These changes may reflect more fine-tuned control of tactile sensation by the vibrissae, and changes in feeding behaviors from neonatal suckling to adult licking and chewing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental changes observed.

claim: The coordinates of all traced premotor neurons are accessible from the source file.
source: The coordinates of all traced premotor neurons are accessible from the source file for interested users.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: Despite efficient transsynaptic labeling, a scarce number of TVA-mCherry and GFP double-positive motoneurons (starter cells) were observed, and the majority of those neurons degenerated.
source: Notably, despite efficient transsynaptic labeling, we often observed a scarce number of TVA-mCherry and GFP double-positive motoneurons, that is, starter cells, and the majority of those neurons degenerated.
evidence: This is an observation about the technical outcome of the tracing method.

claim: The loss of starter cells results from the toxicity of ΔG-RV.
source: This loss of starter cells results from the toxicity of ∆G-RV since omission of RV injection did not cause this problem (data not shown).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on control experiments.
